message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a C++ library PURELY AS A BLACK BOX by running a compiled binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test16_executable
Its C++ driver source is (library source is NOT available - do not look for it):

  int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
      if (argc < 2) return 1;
      std::string url = argv[1];
      std::cout << url_parser::URL::is_valid_url(url) << std::endl;       // LINE 1
      url_parser::URL parser(url);
      std::cout << url_parser::is_scheme_valid(parser.scheme()) << std::endl;  // LINE 2
      std::cout << url_parser::is_host_valid(parser.host()) << std::endl;      // LINE 3
      std::cout << url_parser::is_port_valid(parser.port()) << std::endl;      // LINE 4
      auto path_segments = url_parser::split_path(parser.path());
      std::cout << path_segments.size() << std::endl;                          // LINE 5
      for (const auto& segment : path_segments) std::cout << segment << std::endl;  // LINES 6+
      return 0;
  }

So each run gives you exactly 5 numbers + the path segments. Lines 1-4 are bools printed as 1/0.

KNOWN INTERFACE (from the binary's symbol table - this is all you get):
  namespace url_parser {
    std::string url_decode(const std::string&);
    std::string url_encode(const std::string&);
    std::vector<std::string> split_path(const std::string&);
    bool is_scheme_valid(const std::string&);
    bool is_host_valid(const std::string&);
    bool is_port_valid(int);                 // NOTE: port is an int
    static bool URL::is_valid_url(const std::string&);
    class URL {
      URL(); URL(const std::string&);
      void parse(const std::string&);
      std::string scheme() const; std::string userinfo() const; std::string host() const;
      int port() const; std::string path() const; std::string query() const;
      std::string fragment() const; std::string authority() const;
      bool has_scheme/has_authority/has_userinfo/has_host/has_port/has_path/has_query/has_fragment() const;
      bool is_valid() const;
      ... setters, normalize(), normalize_case(), normalize_path(), normalize_query(), to_string(), operator==
    };
    // internal statics: trim(const std::string&), to_lower(const std::string&),
    //                   is_hex(char), hex_to_char(char)
    // to_lower is implemented as std::transform with a lambda taking (unsigned char)
  }

PROBE HARNESS - use this pattern (handles quoting safely):
  BIN=/workspace/dataset/test16_executable
  probe() { printf '%s => ' "$(printf '%q' "$1")"; "$BIN" "$1" 2>&1 | tr '\n' '|'; printf ' (exit %s)\n' "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; }
  probe 'http://example.com'
  probe $'http://a\tb'        # use $'...' for control chars / tabs / newlines
  probe "$(printf 'http://a\xc3\xa9')"   # for high bytes / UTF-8

You may run HUNDREDS of probes - do it in batches inside one bash call using loops. Be exhaustive and systematic:
sweep single characters, boundary lengths, every ASCII code 0..127 where relevant, high bytes 128..255,
empty strings, and combinations. Isolate one variable at a time.

ESTABLISHED FACTS (already confirmed, do not re-derive, but you MAY correct them if you find contradictions):
  ''                              => 0 0 0 0 0
  'http://example.com'            => 1 1 1 0 0
  'https://localhost:8080'        => 1 1 1 1 0
  'http://example.com/a/b/c'      => 1 1 1 0 3 [a,b,c]
  'http://example.com/a/b/c/'     => 1 1 1 0 3 [a,b,c]
  'http://example.com//a//b'      => 1 1 1 0 2 [a,b]      (empty segments dropped)
  'http://example.com/'           => 1 1 1 0 0
  'example.com'                   => 1 0 0 0 1 [example.com]   (no '://' => whole string is path)
  'http://example.com:0'          => 1 1 1 1 0   (port 0 IS valid => absent port must be a sentinel like -1)
  'http://example.com:65535'      => 1 1 1 1 0
  'http://example.com:65536'      => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:-1'         => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:abc'        => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:'           => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:80abc'      => 1 1 1 1 0   (looks like std::stoi: leading digits, trailing junk ignored)
  'HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B'        => 1 1 1 0 2 [A,B]  (NO case normalization in parse)
  '://example.com'                => 1 0 1 0 0   (scheme='' invalid, host='example.com')
  'http:/example.com'             => 1 0 0 0 2 [http:,example.com]
  'http://'                       => 0 1 0 0 0
  'http:///a/b'                   => 1 1 0 0 2 [a,b]
  'http://:8080'                  => 0 1 0 1 0
  'http://@example.com'           => 1 1 1 0 0   (userinfo split on '@')
  'http://example.com?a=/b/c'     => 1 1 1 0 0   (query stripped before path)
  'http://example.com#/x/y'       => 1 1 1 0 0   (fragment stripped before path)
  'http://example.com/a%20b/c%2Fd'=> 1 1 1 0 2 [a%20b,c%2Fd]  (split_path does NOT url-decode)
  'http://example.com/./../a'     => 1 1 1 0 3 [.,..,a]       (no dot-segment removal)
  'http://exa_mple.com'           => 1 1 0 0 0   (underscore => host INVALID)
  'http://-example.com'           => 1 1 1 0 0   (leading hyphen => host VALID)
  'http://example..com'           => 1 1 1 0 0   (empty label => host VALID)
  'http://[::1]:8080/x'           => 1 1 1 0 1 [x]  (!! port INVALID but host VALID - investigate)
  'http://[::1]/x'                => 1 1 1 0 1 [x]
  'http://ex ample.com'           => 1 1 0 0 0
  ':'                             => 1 0 0 0 1 [:]
  '://'                           => 0 0 0 0 0

A LEADING HYPOTHESIS for line 1 (is_valid_url), which you should test hard if it is in your scope:
  is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty())  after parsing


=== YOUR ASSIGNMENT: input trimming, whitespace, control chars, high bytes ===

Determine (a) whether/where the internal trim() is applied - to the whole URL in parse()? to individual components?
to path segments? - and (b) EXACTLY which characters trim() strips.
The binary imports std::string::find_first_not_of and find_last_not_of, which strongly suggests
trim(s) = s.substr(first_not_of(WS), ...) with a literal WS character set. Determine that set precisely by testing
each candidate character (space 0x20, tab 0x09, LF 0x0A, CR 0x0D, VT 0x0B, FF 0x0C) as a leading and trailing char.
Method: use LINE 5 + segments to read the path back out - e.g. probe $' /a/b ' or $'\thttp://example.com/a\t' and see
whether the whitespace survives into the segments or the host.
Then (c) characterize high bytes 0x80-0xFF: to_lower uses a lambda taking (unsigned char) which suggests the code is
careful about UB; check whether is_host_valid/is_scheme_valid accept high bytes (an isalnum() with the default C
locale rejects them; a hand-rolled a-z/A-Z/0-9 check also rejects them; but a signed-char isalnum could differ).
Test multi-byte UTF-8 in host, scheme, and path. Report exactly what trim strips and how high bytes are treated.

Run as many probes as it takes (hundreds is fine, batch them in loops). Do NOT stop at a plausible rule - push until every boundary is pinned by an actual observed probe result. Then report the rule so precisely that someone can implement it in Rust without ever running the binary. If you find that one of the ESTABLISHED FACTS is wrong, say so in correctionsToEstablishedFacts.

input.dimension: Input trimming, whitespace, control characters, and high bytes (0x80-0xFF)
input.rule:
## PART A — WHERE trim() IS APPLIED: NOWHERE OBSERVABLE

Exhaustive probing (all 255 possible non-NUL bytes swept as a prefix of the URL, as a suffix of the path,
mid-host, mid-scheme, leading/trailing in the port substring, and as the entire input) shows that
`trim()` is **NOT** applied to any of these:

- the whole URL string passed to `URL::URL(const std::string&)` / `URL::parse()`
- the whole URL string passed to the static `URL::is_valid_url()`
- `scheme`      (leading WS before "http" becomes part of the scheme => is_scheme_valid == false)
- `userinfo`
- `host`        (WS adjacent to the host stays in the host => is_host_valid == false)
- `path`        (whole path)
- individual path segments produced by `split_path()`

So for a Rust reimplementation of *this driver's observable behaviour*:
```rust
// parse(), split_path(), is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid() must NEVER trim.
// Every input byte is passed through verbatim; only these bytes are syntactically
// meaningful:  "://"  '/'  '?'  '#'  '@'  ':'  '['  ']'
```
The only two components where a trim call would be *invisible* are:
- the **port** substring: `std::stoi` already skips leading C-locale `isspace`
  (0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20) and one optional '+' / '-', so trim-vs-no-trim is
  behaviourally identical. Both `":"`-only and `": "`-only ports yield port invalid.
- **query** and **fragment**: never printed by the driver.

## PART B — THE EXACT CHARACTER SET OF trim()

Because trim() is not reachable from the driver, its set cannot be derived from behaviour.
It **can** be read off the binary image: at file offset 53432 (0xD0B8) there is the
NUL-terminated literal `20 09 0d 0a 00`, i.e. `" \t\r\n"` (immediately followed by the other
parser literals `"://"`, `"@"`, `":"`, `"/"`, `"?"`, `"#"`, `"&"`, `"="`, `".."`, `"."`).

```rust
const WS: &[char] = &[' ', '\t', '\r', '\n'];   // 0x20, 0x09, 0x0D, 0x0A
fn trim(s: &str) -> &str {
    match s.find(|c| !WS.contains(&c)) {
        None => "",                                  // all-WS  => empty  (find_first_not_of == npos)
        Some(i) => &s[i ..= s.rfind(|c| !WS.contains(&c)).unwrap()],
    }
}
```
Note the set is only FOUR characters. **VT (0x0B) and FF (0x0C) are NOT stripped**, so this is
NOT `isspace`. Order in the literal is space, tab, CR, LF.
(This function is effectively dead code w.r.t. the five printed lines.)

## PART C — OBSERVED WHITESPACE / CONTROL-CHAR BEHAVIOUR (fully black-box)

For every c in {0x20 SP, 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0D CR, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF} the results are
IDENTICAL — there is no special-casing of any whitespace character anywhere:

| input pattern                    | LINE1 | LINE2 scheme | LINE3 host | LINE4 port | LINE5/segments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<c>http://example.com/a/b`      | 1 | **0** | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http<c>://example.com/a/b`      | 1 | **0** | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://<c>example.com/a/b`      | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com<c>/a/b`      | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com:<c>80/a/b`   | 1 | 1 | 1 | **1** | 2 [a,b]  (stoi skips isspace) |
| `http://example.com:80<c>/a/b`   | 1 | 1 | 1 | **1** | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com/<c>a/b`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [**"\<c\>a"**,b] |
| `http://example.com/a<c>/b`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [**"a\<c\>"**,b] |
| `http://example.com/a/b<c>`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,**"b\<c\>"**] |
| `http://<c>u@example.com/a/b`    | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b]  (WS lands in userinfo, ignored) |
| `<c>` alone (whole URL)          | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 [**"\<c\>"**] |

Additional confirmed points:
- 200 leading spaces => scheme invalid; 200 trailing spaces => last segment is `"a"+200 spaces`
  (measured 202 bytes incl. newline). No length cap, no collapsing.
- `$'  \t\r\n  http://example.com/a/b  \t\r\n  '` => `1 0 1 0 2` with segments
  `"a"` and `"b  \t\r\n  "` (embedded LF and all).
- `$'http://example.com/\t/\n/ '` => 3 segments: `"\t"`, `"\n"`, `" "`.
  Whitespace-only segments are NOT empty and are NOT dropped (only truly zero-length segments are).
- `'http:// '` => LINE1=1 (host==" " is non-empty). `' http://'` => LINE1=0 (scheme=" http",
  host=="", path==""). This is strong evidence for no trim in either parse() or is_valid_url().
- Every one of the 255 non-NUL byte values used as the *entire* argument gives `1 0 0 0 1` with
  the byte itself as the single path segment, EXCEPT `'#'`(0x23) and `'?'`(0x3F) => `0 0 0 0 0`
  and `'/'`(0x2F) => `1 0 0 0 0`.
- Byte-suffix sweep on the path: the ONLY bytes that fail to appear verbatim in the last segment
  are 0x23 `#`, 0x2F `/`, 0x3F `?`. All other 252 bytes (including all controls, DEL, and all
  0x80-0xFF) survive byte-exact.

## PART D — HIGH BYTES 0x80-0xFF

`is_host_valid`: rejects **every** byte 0x80-0xFF, plus 0x7F (DEL) and every control 0x01-0x1F,
plus SP. Host-allowed byte set (measured mid-host with `http://exam<B>ple.com/a`) is exactly:
```
A-Z (0x41-0x5A), a-z (0x61-0x7A), 0-9 (0x30-0x39), '-' (0x2D), '.' (0x2E), '[' (0x5B), ']' (0x5D)
```
(bytes 0x23 '#', 0x2F '/', 0x3A ':', 0x3F '?', 0x40 '@' also "pass" only because they truncate the
host before reaching the offending byte). Notably `'_'` 0x5F is rejected, `'~'` 0x7E rejected.
Rejection of high bytes holds at the start of the host, at the end, alone as the whole host, and
inside brackets `http://[<B>]/a`. => The check is ASCII-only and unsigned-char-safe; there is **no**
signed-char/locale `isalnum` leakage.

`is_scheme_valid`: rejects **every** byte 0x80-0xFF, everywhere.
Scheme-allowed set: first char must be `A-Za-z`; subsequent chars `A-Za-z0-9`, `'+'`(0x2B),
`'-'`(0x2D), `'.'`(0x2E). Nothing else, no high bytes.

`split_path` / path: completely byte-transparent, **no** UTF-8 awareness, no percent-decoding,
no validation, no normalisation:
- `http://example.com/caf<C3 A9>/x` => 2 segments, first is the 5 bytes `63 61 66 c3 a9` (verified in hex)
- `http://example.com/<E2 82 AC>/y` => 2 segments [`€`, `y`]
- `http://example.com/<F0 9F 98 80>` => 1 segment (4-byte emoji)
- `http://example.com/<E9>` (lone 0xE9, invalid UTF-8) => 1 segment, 1 byte. No replacement char,
  no error. Segment "length" is a byte count.

Other components with high bytes: userinfo, query and fragment high bytes have zero effect on all
five printed lines. In the port: a high byte *before* the digits makes `stoi` throw =>
port sentinel (-1) => LINE4=0; a high byte *after* the digits is ignored trailing junk => LINE4=1.

`to_lower` (the `(unsigned char)` lambda) is never invoked on the driver's path because
`normalize_case()`/`normalize()` are not called — confirmed by `HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B` => `[A,B]`.

## PART E — LINE 1 hypothesis: CONFIRMED
`is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty())` held on every one of the several hundred probes,
including the whitespace edge cases: `'http:// '`=>1, `' http://'`=>0, `'http:///'`=>1, `'http://:/'`=>1,
`'http://@ '`=>1, `'http://'`/`'http://?q'`/`'http://#f'`/`'http://:'`/`'http://@'`=>0, `' '`=>1.

evidence.why: THE decisive no-trim probe. If trim() ran on the input in parse() or is_valid_url(), the string would become "" and the output would be 0 0 0 0 0 (the known result for ''). It is not.
host==" " is non-empty so LINE1=1; if host were trimmed it would be "" and (with path also "") LINE1 would be 0. Proves host is not trimmed.
LINE2=0: scheme is " http", not "http". Proves the whole-URL string is not left-trimmed. Identical result for leading TAB, LF, CR, VT, FF.

evidence.output: all: 1 1 1 0 2 with last segment = "b"+the whitespace byte (hex-verified: ...62 20 0a / 62 09 0a / 62 0d 0a / 62 0b 0a / 62 0c 0a; LF case verified with $'..' quoting to avoid bash command-substitution stripping)
evidence.why: Proves neither the path nor the segments are right-trimmed, for every one of the 6 whitespace candidates.
Segments keep interior/edge whitespace verbatim; split_path does not trim.
Whitespace-only segments count and are preserved; only zero-length segments are dropped.
host=="example.com<WS>" is invalid; host is not right-trimmed.
scheme=="http<WS>" is invalid; scheme is not right-trimmed.

evidence.output: LINE2 (scheme valid) is 1 only for B in A-Z,a-z; 0 for all 201 other bytes; B='#' and B='?' give 0 0 0 0 0

evidence.input: byte sweep: for B in 0x01..0xFF, argv = 'http://example.com:' + <B> + '80/a'
evidence.why: Exactly std::stoi semantics (C-locale isspace, incl. VT and FF, plus optional '+'). Because this set is a superset of any plausible trim set, a trim() on the port substring is behaviourally unobservable.

evidence.input: byte sweep: for B in 0x01..0xFF, argv = 'http://example.com:80' + <B>
evidence.why: Trailing junk after the digits is ignored by stoi; '@' re-splits the authority so userinfo="example.com:80", host="", port absent.
Byte-exact proof that multi-byte UTF-8 passes through split_path untouched; segment 1 is the 5 bytes 'caf'+C3 A9.
No UTF-8 validation or replacement; segments are raw byte strings.
No IDN/punycode support. 'http://xn--caf-dma.com/x' by contrast gives LINE3=1.
Brackets do not exempt high bytes or DEL from is_host_valid.
High bytes in userinfo/query/fragment are invisible to every printed line.
High byte before digits makes stoi throw (port = absent sentinel); after digits it is ignored.
Long mixed whitespace runs at both ends: nothing stripped at either end, embedded LF preserved inside a segment.

evidence.output: last segment is 201 bytes ("a" + 200 spaces); measured 202 with the newline
evidence.why: No trimming and no length limits on whitespace runs.

SUPPLEMENTARY (binary image, not source): the NUL-terminated trim() whitespace literal is exactly " \t\r\n" — space, tab, CR, LF. VT (0x0B) and FF (0x0C) are absent. It sits directly before the parser's other literals "://", "@", ":", "/", "?", "#", "&", "=", "..", ".".

uncertainties: The exact trim() character set (" \t\r\n", i.e. 0x20/0x09/0x0D/0x0A, WITHOUT VT and FF) could not be established by running the binary, because trim() is not applied to any component the driver can observe. It comes from the NUL-terminated string literal at file offset 53432 in the binary image. Behaviourally the driver is indistinguishable from a build where trim() does not exist at all.

Whether trim() is called on the port substring before std::stoi is undecidable through this driver: stoi already skips all 6 C-locale isspace characters, so both variants give identical LINE4 for every one of the 255 byte values tested at both ends of the port field.
Whether trim() is called on query() / fragment() (or on authority()) is unobservable — the driver never prints them, and they never influence LINE1-LINE5 beyond acting as path terminators.

0x00 (NUL) could not be tested: it cannot be passed through argv. Behaviour on an embedded NUL is unknown (the library takes std::string, so a NUL could in principle be a normal path byte, but this is untested).

is_host_valid accepting '[' (0x5B) and ']' (0x5D) as ordinary host characters (e.g. host "exam[ple.com" is VALID) is a side observation from my byte sweep; the precise bracket/IPv6 parsing rules belong to the host dimension and I did not fully characterise them.
The known oddity 'http://[::1]:8080/x' => port INVALID reproduced exactly, but explaining it is outside this dimension (it is not whitespace- or high-byte-related).
correctionsToEstablishedFacts: No established fact was contradicted; all of them reproduced exactly. One clarification: the assignment's premise that trim() is applied somewhere in the exercised code path is WRONG — trim() is applied to nothing observable (not the URL, not scheme/userinfo/host/path, not path segments). The find_first_not_of / find_last_not_of imports belong to a trim() that this driver never reaches (probably used only by setters/normalize/normalize_query, alongside the also-unreachable "&", "=", "..", "." literals).

Clarification of the established fact 'http://example.com//a//b => 2 segments (empty segments dropped)': only ZERO-LENGTH segments are dropped. Whitespace-only segments are kept, e.g. $'http://example.com/\t/\n/ ' yields 3 segments ["\t", "\n", " "] and 'http://h/ / ' yields 2 segments [" ", " "].

Harness caveat worth recording for anyone re-deriving these facts: bash $(printf '...\x0a') strips trailing newlines, which makes a trailing LF appear to be trimmed. Using $'...\n' quoting shows the LF is in fact preserved in the last path segment.
